nodes.label: PLAN.md — LoRa Messenger Terminal Build Plan
nodes.norm_label: plan.md — lora messenger terminal build plan

nodes.label: Division of Labour — ESP32 Owns Nothing Radio-Shaped
nodes.rationale: The nRF52840 already owns framing, TTL, duplicate suppression, listen-before-talk and retries. The ESP32 is only a terminal: it renders received text, collects outgoing text and speaks one line-based UART protocol. Keeping that boundary sharp is what makes the ESP32 side unit-testable on a PC.
nodes.norm_label: division of labour — esp32 owns nothing radio-shaped

nodes.label: The Pin Assignment Is Forced, Not Chosen
nodes.rationale: Three constraints leave no freedom: TFT_eSPI writes all eight data lines with one 32-bit GPIO register store so no LCD pin can be >= 32; the touch sheet is wired inside the shield onto LCD_RS/LCD_CS and both must be sampled as analog, forcing GPIO25/26 (ADC2_CH8/CH9); nothing else needs a pin. GPIO6-11 (SPI flash), GPIO12 (MTDI strapping) and GPIO2 (onboard LED) are deliberately avoided.
nodes.norm_label: the pin assignment is forced, not chosen

nodes.label: Portrait 240x320 Is TFT_ROTATION 1
nodes.rationale: The panel is an ILI9342 whose native orientation is landscape 320x240, so portrait is rotation 1 — the opposite of a real ILI9341. Portrait was chosen because the inbox gets 254 px of rows instead of 174 and the device reads like a handheld pager.

nodes.label: Rotation-Agnostic Touch Calibration
nodes.rationale: Calibration taps four targets inset 30 px from the corners (a resistive panel is least linear at its edge) and derives from the data whether the raw axes are swapped or inverted, so nothing assumes how the glass is mounted. Calibration is per-orientation and not transferable; TOUCH_CAL_VERSION embeds the rotation so a changed TFT_ROTATION fails to load rather than silently mapping taps wrongly. Result is persisted to NVS.

nodes.label: Touch Is the Only Input
nodes.rationale: Dropping the four push buttons freed four GPIOs, four wires and two resistors, removed an input that could invent an emergency, and removed the lv_group_t focus model a pointer-only UI does not need. The cost is that touch becomes a single point of failure (R4d) and the out-of-band panic path is gone (R4e).

nodes.label: Floating GPIO34 Fired an Unasked-For Panic SOS
nodes.rationale: GPIO34/35 are input-only with no internal pull-up. During Stage 5 an unpulled GPIO34 registered an 800 ms long press by itself and fired a panic SOS. On a device whose whole purpose is emergency traffic, an input that can invent an SOS is worse than no input at all — this episode is why the buttons were removed.
nodes.norm_label: floating gpio34 fired an unasked-for panic sos

nodes.label: ESP32 to nRF Outgoing Line Protocol
nodes.rationale: Works today with no nRF firmware change: serial_poll() accumulates console characters and calls originate() on CR/LF, so the ESP32 only has to write a newline-terminated line.
nodes.norm_label: esp32 to nrf outgoing line protocol

nodes.label: 32-Byte Payload Cap (MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN)
nodes.rationale: Hard constraint imposed by the radio firmware: characters past 32 on a line are silently dropped by the nRF, so the compose screen must enforce a 32-character limit with a visible counter and every preset string must fit.

nodes.label: Path A — Parse the Zephyr Log Line
nodes.rationale: Zero nRF changes, but brittle: breaks on ANSI colour escapes, timestamp format changes, deferred-mode dropped lines, or a lowered log level. Implemented as a fallback only.
nodes.norm_label: path a — parse the zephyr log line

nodes.label: Path B — Machine-Readable +RX/+TX Line
nodes.rationale: About six lines of Zephyr: a printk() alongside the existing LOG_INF emitting +RX,src,seq,rssi,snr,msg and +TX,seq,text. Anything not starting with + is human log noise. Survives log reformatting and gives the UI a real send confirmation instead of a hopeful assumption. The parser is written against Path B and falls back to Path A.

nodes.label: Required Zephyr-Side Console Configuration
nodes.rationale: The console must be a hardware UART, not USB CDC ACM, because the ESP32 cannot be a USB host. Needs CONFIG_LOG_MODE_IMMEDIATE=y, CONFIG_LOG_BACKEND_SHOW_COLOR=n, CONFIG_UART_CONSOLE=y and a board overlay pointing zephyr,console at uart0 at 115200.

nodes.label: Arduino-Free Logic Layer
nodes.rationale: LoraLink's parser and MessageStore contain no Arduino calls — they take bytes and a millisecond count as arguments. That lets pio test -e native run the protocol and UI-state logic on a PC in under a second, so the hardware stages only ever have to prove wiring, not logic.

nodes.label: LVGL v9.5 UI Stack
nodes.rationale: Buys a real widget set (lv_list, lv_textarea, lv_keyboard, lv_msgbox), flexbox layout so screens reflow instead of being pinned to pixel constants, and a scrolling model that already distinguishes a drag from a tap — worth more than it sounds on a noisy resistive sheet.

nodes.label: LVGL Port Layer Is the Only Place That Knows Hardware
nodes.rationale: lib/lvgl_port owns the draw buffer, the flush callback and the tick; screens above it never see TFT_eSPI and never learn the panel is on a parallel bus.
nodes.norm_label: lvgl port layer is the only place that knows hardware

nodes.label: RENDER_MODE_PARTIAL With a Single Draw Buffer
nodes.rationale: DIRECT/FULL want a screen-sized 150 KB buffer, and with a synchronous DMA-less parallel bus there is nothing for a second buffer to overlap with. Measured: 19.2 KB buffer (240x40 RGB565), 30-31 refresh/s at the configured 33 ms cap, LVGL pool 26% of 48 KB, heap flat at 280 KB.
nodes.norm_label: render_mode_partial with a single draw buffer

nodes.label: lv_list_add_button NULL vs Empty-String Trap
nodes.rationale: The widget only skips creating its label on a NULL pointer; an empty string still builds a label, sets LV_LABEL_LONG_MODE_SCROLL_CIRCULAR and gives it flex_grow 1. That invisible label absorbs the row and shoves the real content out of place, and nothing about it looks wrong in the source.

nodes.label: LVGL Default Theme Styles Every Container
nodes.rationale: lv_obj_create arrives with a rounded border, an inset pad and a background, so a stack of containers shows gutters instead of a full-bleed layout. Stripping them is what makeBand() in t1c_lvgl.cpp exists for.
nodes.norm_label: lvgl default theme styles every container

nodes.label: Verified Full-Panel Coverage (Two Independent Checks)
nodes.rationale: "The layout does not reach the edges" and "the port is not addressing the whole panel" look identical on the bench and have nothing to do with each other, so both are measured: band geometry from the widget tree, and lvglPortGetCoverage() accumulating the union of every area handed to the flush callback at the hardware boundary.

nodes.label: Compose Screen
nodes.rationale: lv_textarea plus lv_keyboard with a hard 32-char limit and a live counter. The keyboard is the one place the 40 px touch floor is broken and it is unavoidable: a 10-column QWERTY across 240 px gives 24 px keys, so lv_keyboard_set_popovers() draws the pressed key above the fingertip. This is exactly why presets are the primary send path and free text the fallback.

nodes.label: SOS Alert Screen (full-screen takeover)
nodes.rationale: An incoming message whose text starts with SOS takes over the screen as a red full-screen alert that must be acknowledged, and it still carries SEND MY SOS alongside ACKNOWLEDGE — an incoming emergency is exactly when the operator is most likely to need to raise one of their own.

nodes.label: UI_MIN_TOUCH_PX — 40 px Minimum Touch Target
nodes.rationale: A fingertip on a resistive sheet is not precise and calibration error adds a few pixels. On a 240 px panel that allows one full-width action per row. static_asserts in lib/UI/UI.cpp tie row and footer heights to the constant so a future resize cannot quietly drop below it.

nodes.label: Presets as a Scrolling List, Not a Button Matrix
nodes.rationale: Eight presets sharing a 240 px body would give 30 px rows, under the touch floor, and an lv_buttonmatrix cannot scroll to buy room.
nodes.norm_label: presets as a scrolling list, not a button matrix

nodes.label: SOS Reachable in One Tap From Every Screen
nodes.rationale: Built by the shared chrome rather than by each screen, so no screen can forget it. One tap sends with no confirmation step — that is what the long press on OK did too, and a confirm dialog is what someone under stress cannot deal with. The trade is that a stray tap transmits.
nodes.norm_label: sos reachable in one tap from every screen

nodes.label: A Failed Calibration Boots Into Calibration
nodes.rationale: With no fallback input, a UI drawn on an uncalibrated panel is unreachable, so Touch::loadCal() returning false must route straight into the Stage 2 flow rather than into the inbox. The flow works in raw ADC space and asks for taps at known targets, so it is usable uncalibrated — which is exactly why it can be the recovery path.
nodes.norm_label: a failed calibration boots into calibration

nodes.label: Staged Bring-Up Workflow
nodes.rationale: Each stage is its own PlatformIO environment, flashed and signed off on its own, and no stage begins before the previous stage's exit criteria are met. When the integrated app misbehaves at Stage 7 every layer underneath has already been proven in isolation, so the bug has nowhere to hide and a symptom always has one possible cause.

nodes.label: Stage 1a — Identify the LCD Controller (env t1a_lcdid)
nodes.rationale: These shields ship with any of a dozen controllers behind an identical-looking panel and the silkscreen never says which. The driver is a compile-time choice, so guessing wrong produces a white screen indistinguishable from a wiring fault. Stage 1a settles it by bit-banging the bus, depending on no display library at all.
nodes.norm_label: stage 1a — identify the lcd controller (env t1a_lcdid)

nodes.label: Stage 2 — Touch and Calibration (env t2_touch)
nodes.rationale: With touch the only input, Stage 2 stops being a bring-up step and becomes the thing the product depends on.

nodes.label: Stage 3 — Touch as an LVGL Input Device (env t3_touchui)
nodes.norm_label: stage 3 — touch as an lvgl input device (env t3_touchui)

nodes.label: Stage 4 — UART Link to the nRF (env t4_uart)
nodes.norm_label: stage 4 — uart link to the nrf (env t4_uart)

nodes.label: Stage 5 — LVGL UI on Mock Data (env t5_ui)
nodes.rationale: The entire UI is built against fake messages so it is finished and debugged before the radio is ever attached; at Stage 7 the only new thing in the system is one function call replacing the fake generator.
nodes.norm_label: stage 5 — lvgl ui on mock data (env t5_ui)

nodes.label: Stage 6 — Protocol Layer and Native Tests (pio test -e native)
nodes.norm_label: stage 6 — protocol layer and native tests (pio test -e native)

nodes.label: Stage 8 — Hardening
nodes.rationale: Watchdog, TX queue backpressure, UART-silence detection (nRF not responding), and a brownout check with the backlight at full.

nodes.label: Stage 1a Finding — This Panel Answers No ID Register
nodes.rationale: Registers 0x04, 0xD3 and 0xBF all return only the ESP32's own pin capacitance even though the panel implements the ILI9341 command set perfectly — common on clone shields. It exposed a limit of the tool: probing with an arbitrary command and re-reading cannot distinguish a broken bus from a controller correctly ignoring a non-read command, so a floating-bus report is a hint, never a verdict.
nodes.norm_label: stage 1a finding — this panel answers no id register

nodes.label: Finding — The Controller Is an ILI9342, Not an ILI9341
nodes.rationale: The two parts share an init sequence, a rotation table and a command set and differ only in native geometry (240x320 vs 320x240), so the wrong choice does not fail loudly: the panel initialises, throughput measures 51.7 fps / 3.97 Mpixel/s and the geometry test reports exactly the size the driver was told to expect. It is self-consistent and wrong. The only symptom is at the edges — drawing lands in the left 240 of 320 columns, the bottom 80 rows fall off the glass, and a stale strip down the right side holds fragments of an earlier frame at 90 degrees, which reads as bus corruption.
nodes.norm_label: finding — the controller is an ili9342, not an ili9341

nodes.label: Only Geometry Identifies a Controller
nodes.rationale: Matching a command set does not identify a controller. Only geometry does, and geometry can only be checked against the physical edges of the glass — which is why Stage 1a's register probing could not settle it and Stage 1b's visual check could.

nodes.label: R1 — nRF Console on USB CDC
nodes.rationale: If the Zephyr console is USB CDC the ESP32 can never reach it, because the ESP32 cannot be a USB host. Mitigation is a Zephyr overlay repointing zephyr,console to uart0. Blocks Stage 4 and is the single biggest integration risk.
nodes.norm_label: r1 — nrf console on usb cdc

nodes.label: R2 — 32-Byte Payload Cap Silently Truncates
nodes.rationale: Mitigation: enforce in the compose UI with a live counter and unit-test the boundary.

nodes.label: R3 — Unknown LCD Controller
nodes.rationale: A wrong *_DRIVER flag looks exactly like a wiring fault. Mitigation: Stage 1a identifies it empirically before any driver is compiled.

nodes.label: R4 — Touch Shares Four LCD Lines and Has No Controller
nodes.rationale: Every read reconfigures CS/RS as analog inputs and hand-drives two data lines, leaving the display bus in the wrong state. Mitigation: save/restore pin modes around each read and sample only between frames, never mid-draw. Owned by Stage 2.
nodes.norm_label: r4 — touch shares four lcd lines and has no controller

nodes.label: R4b — Shield Regulator Fed From Its 5V Pin
nodes.rationale: Feeding it 3.3 V yields about 2.2 V and the controller never starts, presenting as a dead bus. Feed 5V from VIN. A minority of shields instead have 5 V input dividers needing the opposite fix, and Stage 1a's failure text distinguishes the two.
nodes.norm_label: r4b — shield regulator fed from its 5v pin

nodes.label: R4c — ADC2 Unavailable While WiFi Is Active
nodes.rationale: This device never enables WiFi, so it is free — but it is a one-way door: the parallel bus has already spent every ADC1 pin, so adding WiFi later would mean giving up touch.
nodes.norm_label: r4c — adc2 unavailable while wifi is active

nodes.label: R4d — Touch Is a Single Point of Failure
nodes.rationale: A lost or corrupt calibration leaves a UI nothing can reach. Boot checks Touch::loadCal() and routes into the Stage 2 calibration flow on failure; the flow itself must be usable uncalibrated.
nodes.norm_label: r4d — touch is a single point of failure

nodes.label: R4e — No Out-of-Band Panic Path
nodes.rationale: A long press on OK used to fire an SOS regardless of what held focus. Mitigation: a persistent on-screen SOS control on every screen, sized at least 40 px, never more than one tap from anywhere.

nodes.label: R5 — Zephyr Log Lines Dropped in Deferred Mode
nodes.rationale: Mitigation: CONFIG_LOG_MODE_IMMEDIATE=y, and prefer Path B.
nodes.norm_label: r5 — zephyr log lines dropped in deferred mode

nodes.label: R6 — 3.3 V Regulator Sag With the TFT at Full Brightness
nodes.rationale: Mitigation: check esp_reset_reason() for brownout during Stage 1; power the TFT from a separate 3.3 V rail if needed.
nodes.norm_label: r6 — 3.3 v regulator sag with the tft at full brightness

nodes.label: R7 — No Delivery Guarantee (Fire-and-Forget Mesh)
nodes.rationale: +TX confirms transmission, not reception, so the UI shows "sent" and never "delivered". An app-level ACK is a possible Stage 9.

nodes.label: Beacon Filtering Into the Status Screen
nodes.rationale: The nRF beacons "hello <n>" every 10 s. The inbox should filter these into the Status screen rather than showing them as messages, because housekeeping traffic would bury real traffic. Deferred to Stage 7.
nodes.norm_label: beacon filtering into the status screen

nodes.label: Finding — The Panel Is RGB-Ordered, Not BGR
nodes.rationale: TFT_eSPI defaults these controllers to BGR, so -DTFT_RGB_ORDER=1 is required or red and blue are exchanged — confirmed: without it the red SOS screen renders blue. The value is compared as a literal, so it must be 1, not a TFT_RGB symbol (which does not exist and evaluates to 0 = BGR).
nodes.norm_label: finding — the panel is rgb-ordered, not bgr

nodes.label: WIRING.md — Wiring, With the Failure Mode Each Wire Causes
nodes.norm_label: wiring.md — wiring, with the failure mode each wire causes

nodes.label: The Shield Must Be Fed 5 V, Not 3.3 V
nodes.rationale: The shield carries its own AMS1117-3.3 regulator fed from its 5V header pin, and that regulator powers the LCD controller and backlight. Put 3.3 V into it and you get roughly 2.2 V out, the controller never comes out of reset, and every diagnostic reads back 0xFF. The shield's 3V3 pin is the regulator's output and must be left unconnected.
nodes.norm_label: the shield must be fed 5 v, not 3.3 v

nodes.label: The 5 V Input-Divider Shield Variant
nodes.rationale: A minority of these shields put 5V-to-3.3V resistor dividers on the logic inputs assuming a 5 V host; driving those with 3.3 V leaves about 2.2 V at the controller, possibly under its input threshold. Symptom is Stage 1a reading 0xFF everywhere with power verified correct. Fix is the opposite of the usual one: feed the shield's 3V3 pin and leave 5V unconnected.

nodes.label: D8/D9 Crossover — They Carry LCD_D0 and LCD_D1
nodes.rationale: The single most common miswire: the shield's header pins D8 and D9 carry LCD_D0 and LCD_D1 while D2-D7 carry LCD_D2-LCD_D7, so the numbering does not line up. Symptom is unstable garbage from Stage 1a.
nodes.norm_label: d8/d9 crossover — they carry lcd_d0 and lcd_d1

nodes.label: Touch Costs Zero Extra Wires
nodes.rationale: The bare 4-wire resistive sheet's four corners are already wired inside the shield onto lines the LCD uses: XP=LCD_D0, XM=LCD_RS, YP=LCD_CS, YM=LCD_D1. The whole user interface therefore costs no additional GPIO.

nodes.label: Touch Corners Must Land on ADC2 Channels 8 and 9
nodes.rationale: LCD_RS and LCD_CS are on GPIO25/26 specifically because they are ADC2_CH8/CH9 and are sampled as analog voltages; any other assignment would leave the touch panel unreadable.
nodes.norm_label: touch corners must land on adc2 channels 8 and 9

nodes.label: Push Buttons Removed From the Design
nodes.rationale: There are none; touch is the only input and needs no wires. Previously four switches on GPIO32-35 plus two 10k resistors. If kept wired, the resistors must be fitted: GPIO34/35 are input-only with no internal pull-up and drift when floating. Freed GPIO32, 33, 34, 35.
nodes.norm_label: push buttons removed from the design

nodes.label: nRF52840 Link — Cross-Wired UART, Common Ground
nodes.rationale: TX goes to RX (GPIO17 to nRF RX, GPIO16 from nRF TX) at 115200 8N1, and the grounds must be common or the line has no reference and produces garbage bytes. Both parts are 3.3 V logic, so no level shifter; if the nRF has its own supply, connect grounds only.
nodes.norm_label: nrf52840 link — cross-wired uart, common ground

nodes.label: Incremental Wiring Build Order
nodes.rationale: Wire only what the current stage needs: 15 wires carry Stages 1a through 3 (touch and LVGL input add nothing at all), and only Stage 4 adds TX/RX/GND for 18 total.

nodes.label: Failure-Mode Troubleshooting Table
nodes.rationale: Maps each observable symptom to one cause and one fix: 0xFF everywhere is an unpowered shield, 0x0000 is a shorted data line or swapped CS/RS, unstable garbage is the D8/D9 crossover, a left-75% image with a stale right strip is an ILI9342 driven as an ILI9341, red showing blue is the RGB order, and regular vertical stripes name the disconnected bit by their spacing (2 px = D1, 16 px = D4).

nodes.label: Backlight Hardwired to the Shield's 3.3 V Rail
nodes.rationale: There is no control pin on the Uno headers, so brightness is fixed, no GPIO is spent and the GPIO-current hazard an SPI module would have posed is gone. Idle dimming is therefore unavailable and the idle timeout blanks to a dark screen instead.
nodes.norm_label: backlight hardwired to the shield's 3.3 v rail

nodes.label: GPIO5/GPIO15 Strapping Pins Block Download Mode
nodes.rationale: Both are strapping pins and both carry LCD lines; something holding either low at boot stops the board entering download mode. Fix is to unplug the shield and retry.
nodes.norm_label: gpio5/gpio15 strapping pins block download mode

nodes.label: kWdtTimeoutS — Task Watchdog
nodes.rationale: This device's whole job is showing an emergency message, so a wedged UI that still looks alive is the worst failure available; a stall past the timeout reboots into a working terminal instead.

nodes.label: MAX_PAYLOAD_LEN — 32-Byte Payload Limit
nodes.rationale: Also the maximum length of a line typed on the console for the serial bridge. This one constant constrains the whole ESP32 UI: the compose counter, every preset string, and the parser's truncation boundary.

nodes.label: uart_dev = DT_CHOSEN(zephyr_console)
nodes.rationale: The serial bridge speaks over whatever the devicetree chose as the console, so on a board whose console is USB CDC the ESP32 can never reach it — the ESP32 cannot be a USB host. This single line is risk R1.

nodes.label: Listen-Before-Talk Collision Avoidance
nodes.rationale: A relay transmits the moment it decides to and lora_send() backs off with -EBUSY if the channel is busy, rather than blocking in a deaf sleep beforehand. This keeps the node listening right up to the instant it talks, which matters for a star-mesh where one hub relays for several leaves. Five retries at 200 ms backoff.

nodes.label: kKnown[] — Controller ID Table
nodes.rationale: ILI9342 is deliberately given its own entry and must NOT be mapped onto the ILI9341 flag: they share an init sequence and command set but their native geometry differs, and the wrong one draws into the left 240 columns of a 320-wide panel while the bottom 80 rows fall off, with no other symptom.
